title: CS Quest 3.3 · Our class survey (Collect, chart, claim)
name: Our class survey (Collect, chart, claim)
summary: Students design a three-question survey with one deliberately leading question to fix, collect answers from the class, clean and chart them in Data Detective's My Data, and compare with another class by percent. Every pair's chart is pooled on the projector so the class sees what a bigger sample says. One device per student, surveys run in pairs.
iCan: design a short survey and fix a leading question
collect, clean and chart answers from many people
report a finding and compare groups of different sizes by percent
materials: blank survey slips (one per student per question)
doNow: Vote on the board with one tally mark: dog, cat, other or none. Then write one survey question that pushes people toward an answer.
plan: Explore: My Data with the Do Now tallies, then the other class by percent

warmup.why: two retrieval items from 3.2, one vocabulary item, one preview of today, one more from 3.2

do: Open Data Detective at My Data on the projector (Open game at this chapter). Count the Do Now tallies with the class, enter them with the steppers and choose a chart.
Load the provided set from another class and compare the two charts by percent. Read two Do Now questions out loud and ask the class which one is leading.
say: Real data comes from real people. Collecting it well is half the job.
A question that pushes people toward one answer is a leading question. It builds bias into the data before anyone counts.
ask: Our class and the other class are different sizes. Can we compare the dog counts directly? What should we compare instead?
explore.afterAsk: Take answers until someone says percent. Work one out on the board: count divided by the number of respondents, times 100.
explore.bigIdea: A fair finding needs fair questions, clean data and a big enough sample.

play.goal: one survey question charted, cleaned and compared by percent
play.stretch: the chapter: all three questions, then a finding that uses two charts
play.solo: pairs write three questions, fix the leading one and run the survey together on slips (or as one live round); each partner enters the tallies on their own device so both charts can be pooled
lookFors: a leading question kept because it gives the answer the pair wanted
missing or doubled slips not cleaned before charting
comparing counts with the other class instead of percents
play.misconception: More answers do not fix a biased question: a leading question makes the data unfair before anyone counts, so fix the question first.
earlyFinishers: help a neighbor without touching their screen

discuss: Which question was leading, and how did you fix it?
We pooled every pair's chart. Did the pooled chart say the same thing as yours? Why is a bigger sample fairer?
showMe: Every pair's chart for the shared question goes up on the projector, one after another, then the class adds them into one pooled chart.

exit.sentencePrompt: What did your survey find, and what makes the finding fair or not fair?
exit.frame: Our survey found ___; it is fair because ___.

exit.paper: exit half-sheet (two per page) with the three items and the sentence frame

support: two provided questions and one leading question to fix
a printed percent strip: count, total, percent
a tally sheet with the categories filled in
stretch: a finding that uses two charts
run one question as a live round and compare it with the paper answers

unpluggedTwin.title: Tally and Grid
steps: Pairs write three questions; the teacher checks that one leading question was spotted and fixed.
They survey the class on slips and tally the answers.
They clean the slips: blanks, doubles and impossible answers.
They chart one question on grid paper and work out each percent.
Share: tape every chart for the shared question on the board and add them into one pooled chart.

subPlan: Do Now on paper, 3 minutes: vote with one tally mark for a favorite pet, then write one survey question that pushes people toward an answer

Play Data Detective, chapter My Data, on your own for 20 minutes. Classes, then the lesson, then Play. If the game asks, the quest code is 7 2 2 0. Goal: one survey question charted, cleaned and compared by percent. No warm-up and no projector needed; playing signed out is fine.
Paper exit ticket: the half-sheet with three questions and the sentence frame. Collect it.

shortPeriod40.discuss: Which question was leading, and how did you fix it?
shortPeriod40.keep: the exit ticket is never cut

add: one question as a live round before Play
10 minutes of the Unit 3 review on Brain Board

notes: A no-right-answer poll does not exist in the live sets yet; a live round from the Would You Rather topics can stand in for one question.
No names on the slips: the survey counts answers, not people.
Vocabulary beyond the five on the learn card: tally, category, crowdsourcing, leading question.
One device per student at this band.

steps.title: Today
steps.body:
Do Now: Vote on the board with one tally mark: dog, cat, other or none. Then write one survey question that pushes people toward an answer.

Big idea: A fair finding needs fair questions, clean data and a big enough sample.

We will talk about:
- Which question was leading, and how did you fix it?
- We pooled every pair's chart. Did the pooled chart say the same thing as yours? Why is a bigger sample fairer?

steps.title: Warm-up (live)
steps.body: Five quick questions. Your teacher shows them on the projector or starts them live.

steps.title: Play: My Data
steps.body:
Goal: one survey question charted, cleaned and compared by percent. Stretch: chart all three questions, then write a finding that uses two charts.
If the game asks for a quest code, it is 7 2 2 0.
Pairs write the survey and collect the answers together. Fix the leading question before you hand it out. Each of you enters the numbers on your own device.

steps.title: Exit ticket
steps.body: Three quick questions about surveys, bias and pooling.

steps.title: In your own words
steps.body:
What did your survey find, and what makes the finding fair or not fair?
Frame: Our survey found ___; it is fair because ___.
